summary: DeepSeek and MiniMax get approval to offer their AI abroad and DeepSeek works with Huawei on chips, while young Chinese travellers embrace cheap 'disposable outfits'.
body: China's AI developers DeepSeek and MiniMax have received state approval to offer their AI models for use around the world, according to a social media account linked to state broadcaster CCTV, as reported by Reuters [^1]. Neither company had commented [^1]. The news follows China's October 16 proposal for export controls on 23 kinds of AI technology; the commerce ministry says most AI will remain exportable and that licensing for open-source technology will be simplified [^1]. Separately, The Information reports that Huawei engineers are working in DeepSeek's offices to help design future Huawei AI chips around DeepSeek's models, as reported by Investing.com [^2]. DeepSeek plans to start training on Huawei's Ascend 950DT chips as early as the end of 2026, but the research group Epoch AI estimates Nvidia's top chip has about seven times the raw computing power of the Ascend 950, and DeepSeek still wants access to Nvidia chips [^2]. My read: China is trying to make its AI both more independent of U.S. chips and more widely used abroad, under state control of what leaves the country.

In daily life, Sixth Tone reports that young Chinese travellers have taken up cipaoyi, or "disposable outfits": cheap clothes, often under 50 yuan (about US$7) per item, bought for a trip or photo shoot, worn once and then thrown away or resold [^3]. The trend took off during this month's National Day holiday, and posts about it on Douyin, China's version of TikTok, have drawn more than 60 million views [^3]. One 20-year-old student told Sixth Tone she resells used outfits online to cover costs [^3]. Dermatologists warn that cheap fabrics can irritate skin, and a Shanghai recycler said the textiles it collected over the holiday nearly doubled from last year, many of them synthetic blends that are hard to recycle [^3]. A China circular-economy association expects discarded clothing to reach 50 million tonnes a year by 2030 [^3].

reads.title: In Stitches: Why Young Chinese Are Buying Clothes They Can Throw Away
reads.summary: A lively look at the 'disposable outfit' trend: why young travellers buy clothes to wear once, and the costs to skin, budgets and the environment.
